# Introduction

::: callout-important
**We call this method NLA-GP:** Nested-Library Analysis ([Huang et al. 2024](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011759)), with [GP-EDM](https://github.com/tanyalrogers/GPEDM) (Munch et al. 2017) instead of the original S-map.
:::

## Background

::: callout-note
NLA answers one question:

> Does a time series show a change point (regime shift)?
:::

How it works:

- Reconstruct the system's dynamics from a time series (via EDM)
- Gradually remove older data ("shrink the library")
- Find the point where prediction accuracy improves the most
- That point is the regime shift: older data comes from a different dynamical regime and actively harms prediction

Huang et al. 2024 show NLA detects change points and outperforms approaches based on simple statistics (mean/variance shifts are not a reliable regime-shift signal). Their original code (S-map based) is [on GitHub](https://github.com/chromian/Nested-Library-Analysis).

## Goal

Replace S-map with GP-EDM inside the NLA framework, per tips from Steve Munch & Tanya Rogers (GP-EDM's authors):

- Fit GP-EDM in **two stages**: hyperparameters are slow to fit, but predicting with them fixed is fast
- To change the training data while keeping hyperparameters fixed: refit with `fitGP()`, passing the previous `pars` as `fixedpars` -- this skips the slow optimization step
- A matrix inversion is still needed whenever the training data changes, but that's cheap

::: callout-warning
**Decision:** we implement NLA-GP using this two-stage approach, and compare it against the original NLA-S-map.
:::

## Algorithm

Huang et al. 2024 give NLA as two symmetric algorithms ([S1 Text](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011759.s001)): fix a test set at one end of the series, and repeatedly shrink the library at the other end.

### Steps

1. Fix a test set and an initial library
2. For every possible **outer** library start `n`: fit hyperparameters once, using library `{n, ..., L}` to predict the test set
3. Holding those hyperparameters fixed, shrink the library from an **inner** start `l` (`l` from `n` to `L`), recording out-of-sample error as a curve `E_n(l)`
4. Smooth `E_n(.)`; if it's valley-shaped, its minimum is a candidate change point `tau_n`
5. Final estimate: the median of all the `tau_n`

### Left check

Test set = the **last** part of the series. Library shrinks by removing the **oldest** data first (from the start). Finds a shift located in the **early** part of the series.

### Right check

Test set = the **first** part of the series. Library shrinks by removing the **newest** data first (from the end). Finds a shift located in the **late** part of the series.

### Discriminant

A curve is "valley-shaped" exactly when (Huang et al. 2024, Methods, Sec. 2.2):

$$
\frac{d\tilde{\varepsilon}}{dl}(t) < 0 \text{ for } t < \tau, \qquad \frac{d\tilde{\varepsilon}}{dl}(t) > 0 \text{ for } t > \tau
$$

i.e. error strictly decreases while misleading (different-regime) data is still being removed, then strictly increases once only correct (same-regime) data is left to remove. We detect this as a single run of negative differences followed by a single run of positive differences in the smoothed curve.

### Code

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**This section implements the algorithm above:**

- `nla_left()` / `nla_right()`: left check / right check
- Two-stage fit: hyperparameters fit once per outer `n`, reused via `fixedpars` while the library shrinks further
- `smooth_gaussian()` + `find_valley()`: smooth the error curve and apply the discriminant above
- Scaling is fixed once, over the whole series (not recomputed per library size), so `fixedpars` stay valid as the library shrinks
:::

```{r core_functions}
#' Gaussian-kernel smoothing of an error curve (the paper's "Gaussian filter").
#' bandwidth is in units of the index spacing (Dskipstep).
smooth_gaussian <- function(idx, y, bandwidth) {
  keep <- is.finite(y)
  if (sum(keep) < 3) return(rep(NA_real_, length(y)))
  out <- rep(NA_real_, length(y))
  xi <- idx[keep]; yi <- y[keep]
  for (i in seq_along(idx)) {
    w <- exp(-0.5 * ((xi - idx[i]) / bandwidth)^2)
    out[i] <- sum(w * yi) / sum(w)
  }
  out
}

#' Is a (smoothed) error curve valley-shaped, and if so, where is the minimum?
#' Discriminant (Huang et al. 2024, Sec 2.2): the sign sequence of the first
#' difference must be a single run of "-" followed by a single run of "+",
#' with the minimum in the interior.
find_valley <- function(idx, y_smooth, flat_tol = 1e-8) {
  ok <- is.finite(y_smooth)
  if (sum(ok) < 3) return(list(is_valley = FALSE, tau_hat = NA_real_))
  idx <- idx[ok]; y_smooth <- y_smooth[ok]
  o <- order(idx); idx <- idx[o]; y_smooth <- y_smooth[o]

  d <- diff(y_smooth)
  scale_ <- max(abs(y_smooth), flat_tol)
  s <- ifelse(abs(d) < flat_tol * scale_, 0, sign(d))
  s_nz <- s[s != 0]
  if (length(s_nz) < 2) return(list(is_valley = FALSE, tau_hat = NA_real_))

  runs <- rle(s_nz)$values
  is_valley <- length(runs) == 2 && identical(runs, c(-1, 1))

  imin <- which.min(y_smooth)
  at_boundary <- imin == 1 || imin == length(y_smooth)
  is_valley <- is_valley && !at_boundary

  list(is_valley = is_valley, tau_hat = if (is_valley) idx[imin] else NA_real_)
}

#' Build lag/predictor columns ONCE over the full series, and z-score them
#' ONCE using a fixed reference. fitGP(scaling="global") would otherwise
#' recompute mean/sd from whatever subset it's given, silently invalidating
#' fixedpars as the library shrinks -- so we scale up front and always use
#' scaling="none" below.
build_lag_frame <- function(y, E, tau) {
  T <- length(y)
  base <- data.frame(time = seq_len(T), y = y)
  lagdf <- makelags(data = base, y = "y", E = E, tau = tau, append = TRUE)
  xnames <- setdiff(names(lagdf), c("time", "y"))

  complete <- stats::complete.cases(lagdf[, c("y", xnames)])
  ymean <- mean(lagdf$y[complete]); ysd <- sd(lagdf$y[complete])
  lagdf$y <- (lagdf$y - ymean) / ysd
  for (xn in xnames) {
    xmean <- mean(lagdf[[xn]][complete]); xsd <- sd(lagdf[[xn]][complete])
    lagdf[[xn]] <- (lagdf[[xn]] - xmean) / xsd
  }
  list(lagdf = lagdf, xnames = xnames)
}

#' Fit GP hyperparameters on library rows [lib_start, lib_end] and evaluate
#' out-of-sample RMSE on test_rows.
fit_hyperparams <- function(lagdf, xnames, lib_start, lib_end, test_rows) {
  train <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= lib_start & lagdf$time <= lib_end, ]
  tryCatch(
    fitGP(data = train, y = "y", x = xnames, scaling = "none", newdata = test_rows),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
}

#' Refit with hyperparameters fixed (2-stage trick): only a matrix inversion
#' for the new (smaller) library is recomputed.
refit_fixed <- function(lagdf, xnames, lib_start, lib_end, test_rows, fixedpars) {
  train <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= lib_start & lagdf$time <= lib_end, ]
  if (nrow(na.omit(train[, c("y", xnames)])) < length(xnames) + 2) return(NA_real_)
  fit <- tryCatch(
    fitGP(data = train, y = "y", x = xnames, scaling = "none",
          fixedpars = fixedpars, newdata = test_rows),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) return(NA_real_)
  unname(fit$outsampfitstats["rmse"])
}

#' Left check (Algorithm 1): library = y[1:L], test = y[(L+1):R].
nla_left <- function(y, L, R = length(y), E = 3, tau = 1, Dskipstep = 5,
                      bandwidth = 2 * Dskipstep, min_lib = E * tau + 3) {
  lf <- build_lag_frame(y, E, tau)
  lagdf <- lf$lagdf; xnames <- lf$xnames
  test_rows <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= (L + 1) & lagdf$time <= R, ]

  n_seq <- seq(0, L - min_lib, by = Dskipstep)
  tau_n <- rep(NA_real_, length(n_seq))
  curves <- vector("list", length(n_seq))

  for (i in seq_along(n_seq)) {
    n <- n_seq[i]
    lib_start_n <- max(1, n)
    hp <- fit_hyperparams(lagdf, xnames, lib_start_n, L, test_rows)
    if (is.null(hp)) next
    fixedpars <- hp$pars[seq_len(length(xnames) + 2)]

    l_seq <- seq(n, L - min_lib, by = Dskipstep)
    if (length(l_seq) < 3) next
    err <- vapply(l_seq, function(l) {
      refit_fixed(lagdf, xnames, max(1, l), L, test_rows, fixedpars)
    }, numeric(1))

    y_smooth <- smooth_gaussian(l_seq, err, bandwidth)
    v <- find_valley(l_seq, y_smooth)
    tau_n[i] <- v$tau_hat
    curves[[i]] <- data.frame(n = n, l = l_seq, rmse = err, rmse_smooth = y_smooth)
  }

  list(tau_hat = if (all(is.na(tau_n))) NA_real_ else median(tau_n, na.rm = TRUE),
       tau_n = data.frame(n = n_seq, tau_hat = tau_n),
       curves = do.call(rbind, curves))
}

#' Right check (Algorithm 2): test = y[1:L], library = y[(L+1):R].
nla_right <- function(y, L, R = length(y), E = 3, tau = 1, Dskipstep = 5,
                       bandwidth = 2 * Dskipstep, min_lib = E * tau + 3) {
  lf <- build_lag_frame(y, E, tau)
  lagdf <- lf$lagdf; xnames <- lf$xnames
  test_rows <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= 1 & lagdf$time <= L, ]

  n_seq <- seq(R, L + 1 + min_lib, by = -Dskipstep)
  tau_n <- rep(NA_real_, length(n_seq))
  curves <- vector("list", length(n_seq))

  for (i in seq_along(n_seq)) {
    n <- n_seq[i]
    hp <- fit_hyperparams(lagdf, xnames, L + 1, n, test_rows)
    if (is.null(hp)) next
    fixedpars <- hp$pars[seq_len(length(xnames) + 2)]

    l_seq <- seq(n, L + 1 + min_lib, by = -Dskipstep)
    if (length(l_seq) < 3) next
    err <- vapply(l_seq, function(l) {
      refit_fixed(lagdf, xnames, L + 1, l, test_rows, fixedpars)
    }, numeric(1))

    y_smooth <- smooth_gaussian(l_seq, err, bandwidth)
    v <- find_valley(l_seq, y_smooth)
    tau_n[i] <- v$tau_hat
    curves[[i]] <- data.frame(n = n, l = l_seq, rmse = err, rmse_smooth = y_smooth)
  }

  list(tau_hat = if (all(is.na(tau_n))) NA_real_ else median(tau_n, na.rm = TRUE),
       tau_n = data.frame(n = n_seq, tau_hat = tau_n),
       curves = do.call(rbind, curves))
}
```

# Synthetic test

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Take a system simple enough to know, exactly, when and why a regime shift happens. Does NLA-GP find it -- and does it do so more accurately, or faster, than the original NLA-S-map?
:::

## Setup

**To answer this, we:**

- Simulate a 2-species predator-prey model (Rosenzweig-MacArthur)
- Slowly ramp its carrying capacity `K` from 2 to 4
- This crosses a textbook bifurcation ("paradox of enrichment") at `K = 3`: the system shifts from a stable equilibrium to a growing limit cycle -- exactly halfway through the series
- Run NLA-GP and NLA-S-map (left and right check, both) on the prey series, and compare

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**This section simulates the synthetic benchmark:**

- 2-species predator-prey model with a slowly ramped carrying capacity
- Adds process noise (random shocks) and measurement noise
- `true_changepoint()`: the known bifurcation time, to score both methods against
:::

```{r regime_shift_functions}
# dV/dt = r V (1 - V/K) - a V P / (1 + a h V)
# dP/dt = e a V P / (1 + a h V) - m P
# K(t)  = K_lo + (K_hi - K_lo) * t / Tmax
#
# With r=1, a=1.1, h=0.8, e=0.7, m=0.4 (textbook values), the coexistence
# equilibrium is stable for K < K_crit = 3.0 and unstable (-> limit cycle)
# above it (found by bisection on simulated oscillation amplitude).
# Ramping K from 2.0 to 4.0 crosses K_crit exactly halfway through.

rm_rhs <- function(t, state, params) {
  with(as.list(c(state, params)), {
    K <- K_lo + (K_hi - K_lo) * t / Tmax
    dV <- r * V * (1 - V / K) - a * V * P / (1 + a * h * V)
    dP <- e * a * V * P / (1 + a * h * V) - m * P
    list(c(V = dV, P = dP))
  })
}

default_rm_params <- function(K_lo = 2, K_hi = 4, Tmax = 500) {
  list(r = 1, a = 1.1, h = 0.8, e = 0.7, m = 0.4, K_lo = K_lo, K_hi = K_hi, Tmax = Tmax)
}

#' Simulate the model with Poisson-arrival process shocks and Gaussian
#' measurement noise.
simulate_regime_shift <- function(Tmax = 500, dt_sample = 1, lambda = 0.01,
                                   rho = 0.05, meas_sd = 0.02,
                                   params = default_rm_params(Tmax = Tmax),
                                   seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n_events <- rpois(1, lambda * Tmax)
  event_times <- sort(runif(n_events, 1e-6, Tmax - 1e-6))
  shocks <- matrix(runif(2 * n_events, 1 - rho, 1 + rho), ncol = 2)
  event_func <- function(t, state, params) {
    i <- which(abs(event_times - t) < 1e-6)[1]
    if (!is.na(i)) state <- pmax(state * shocks[i, ], 1e-6)
    state
  }

  samp_times <- seq(0, Tmax, by = dt_sample)
  sol <- ode(y = c(V = 1, P = 0.5), times = samp_times, func = rm_rhs, parms = params,
             method = "ode45",
             events = if (n_events > 0) list(func = event_func, time = event_times) else NULL)
  traj <- as.data.frame(sol)
  traj <- traj[complete.cases(traj), ]

  traj$K <- with(params, K_lo + (K_hi - K_lo) * traj$time / Tmax)
  for (v in c("V", "P")) {
    traj[[v]] <- scale(traj[[v]])[, 1] + rnorm(nrow(traj), 0, meas_sd)
  }
  rownames(traj) <- NULL
  traj
}

#' True change-point index: the row where K(t) crosses K_crit.
true_changepoint <- function(traj, K_crit = 3.0) {
  which.min(abs(traj$K - K_crit))
}
```

```{r fig-synthetic-traj}
#| fig-cap: "Simulated regime shift: prey abundance V (top) shifts from a stable equilibrium to a growing limit cycle exactly when carrying capacity K (bottom) crosses the bifurcation threshold (blue dotted line)."
traj <- simulate_regime_shift(seed = 1)
cp_true <- true_changepoint(traj)

traj %>%
  select(time, V, K) %>%
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = traj$time[cp_true], linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(data = tibble(variable = "K", value = 3), aes(yintercept = value),
             linetype = "dotted", color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## GP result

```{r run_synthetic_gp}
E <- 3; tau <- 1; Dskipstep <- 8; bandwidth <- 16
T_syn <- nrow(traj)
y_syn <- traj$V

t0 <- Sys.time()
left_gp  <- nla_left(y_syn,  L = 350, R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
right_gp <- nla_right(y_syn, L = 150, R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
time_gp <- as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs")
combined_gp <- median(c(left_gp$tau_hat, right_gp$tau_hat), na.rm = TRUE)

tibble(estimate = c("True change point", "Left check", "Right check", "Combined"),
       value = c(cp_true, left_gp$tau_hat, right_gp$tau_hat, combined_gp))
```

```{r fig-synthetic-curves}
#| fig-cap: "Right-check NLA-GP error curves for a few outer starting points n. Grey: raw RMSE. Blue: smoothed. Dashed red: true change point."
n_show <- unique(right_gp$curves$n) %>% sort() %>% { .[round(seq(1, length(.), length.out = 4))] }
right_gp$curves %>%
  filter(n %in% n_show) %>%
  ggplot(aes(l, rmse)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = rmse_smooth), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = traj$time[cp_true], linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Library start l", y = "Out-of-sample RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Smap result

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**This section implements the original NLA-S-map**, following Huang et al. 2024's S2 Text: a locally-weighted linear regression around each predictee, with kernel weight `w(d) = exp(-theta * d / dbar)`. `theta` plays the same role as the GP hyperparameters above -- fit once per outer `n`, reused (unchanged) while the library shrinks further.
:::

```{r smap_functions}
smap_predict <- function(train_x, train_y, test_x, theta, k = NULL) {
  E <- ncol(train_x)
  if (is.null(k)) k <- E + 1
  N <- nrow(train_x)
  Xtrain1 <- cbind(1, train_x)
  preds <- numeric(nrow(test_x))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(test_x))) {
    xq <- test_x[i, ]
    d <- sqrt(rowSums((train_x - matrix(xq, N, E, byrow = TRUE))^2))
    dbar <- mean(sort(d)[seq_len(min(k, N))])
    if (dbar <= 0) dbar <- 1e-8
    w <- exp(-theta * d / dbar)
    fit <- tryCatch(lm.wfit(x = Xtrain1, y = train_y, w = w), error = function(e) NULL)
    preds[i] <- if (is.null(fit) || any(!is.finite(fit$coefficients))) NA_real_ else sum(c(1, xq) * fit$coefficients)
  }
  preds
}

fit_smap_theta <- function(train_x, train_y, test_x, test_y) {
  obj <- function(theta) sqrt(mean((test_y - smap_predict(train_x, train_y, test_x, theta))^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  optimize(obj, interval = c(1e-4, 10))$minimum
}

fit_hyperparams_smap <- function(lagdf, xnames, lib_start, lib_end, test_rows) {
  train <- na.omit(lagdf[lagdf$time >= lib_start & lagdf$time <= lib_end, c("y", xnames)])
  test <- na.omit(test_rows[, c("y", xnames)])
  if (nrow(train) < length(xnames) + 2 || nrow(test) == 0) return(NULL)
  list(theta = fit_smap_theta(as.matrix(train[, xnames]), train$y, as.matrix(test[, xnames]), test$y))
}

refit_fixed_smap <- function(lagdf, xnames, lib_start, lib_end, test_rows, theta) {
  train <- na.omit(lagdf[lagdf$time >= lib_start & lagdf$time <= lib_end, c("y", xnames)])
  test <- na.omit(test_rows[, c("y", xnames)])
  if (nrow(train) < length(xnames) + 2 || nrow(test) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  p <- smap_predict(as.matrix(train[, xnames]), train$y, as.matrix(test[, xnames]), theta)
  sqrt(mean((test$y - p)^2, na.rm = TRUE))
}

#' Left/right check, with S-map instead of GP-EDM (same nla_left/nla_right
#' structure, so the two methods are compared apples-to-apples).
nla_left_smap <- function(y, L, R = length(y), E = 3, tau = 1, Dskipstep = 5,
                           bandwidth = 2 * Dskipstep, min_lib = E * tau + 3) {
  lf <- build_lag_frame(y, E, tau)
  lagdf <- lf$lagdf; xnames <- lf$xnames
  test_rows <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= (L + 1) & lagdf$time <= R, ]
  n_seq <- seq(0, L - min_lib, by = Dskipstep)
  tau_n <- rep(NA_real_, length(n_seq))
  for (i in seq_along(n_seq)) {
    n <- n_seq[i]
    hp <- fit_hyperparams_smap(lagdf, xnames, max(1, n), L, test_rows)
    if (is.null(hp)) next
    l_seq <- seq(n, L - min_lib, by = Dskipstep)
    if (length(l_seq) < 3) next
    err <- vapply(l_seq, function(l) refit_fixed_smap(lagdf, xnames, max(1, l), L, test_rows, hp$theta), numeric(1))
    v <- find_valley(l_seq, smooth_gaussian(l_seq, err, bandwidth))
    tau_n[i] <- v$tau_hat
  }
  list(tau_hat = if (all(is.na(tau_n))) NA_real_ else median(tau_n, na.rm = TRUE))
}

nla_right_smap <- function(y, L, R = length(y), E = 3, tau = 1, Dskipstep = 5,
                            bandwidth = 2 * Dskipstep, min_lib = E * tau + 3) {
  lf <- build_lag_frame(y, E, tau)
  lagdf <- lf$lagdf; xnames <- lf$xnames
  test_rows <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= 1 & lagdf$time <= L, ]
  n_seq <- seq(R, L + 1 + min_lib, by = -Dskipstep)
  tau_n <- rep(NA_real_, length(n_seq))
  for (i in seq_along(n_seq)) {
    n <- n_seq[i]
    hp <- fit_hyperparams_smap(lagdf, xnames, L + 1, n, test_rows)
    if (is.null(hp)) next
    l_seq <- seq(n, L + 1 + min_lib, by = -Dskipstep)
    if (length(l_seq) < 3) next
    err <- vapply(l_seq, function(l) refit_fixed_smap(lagdf, xnames, L + 1, l, test_rows, hp$theta), numeric(1))
    v <- find_valley(l_seq, smooth_gaussian(l_seq, err, bandwidth))
    tau_n[i] <- v$tau_hat
  }
  list(tau_hat = if (all(is.na(tau_n))) NA_real_ else median(tau_n, na.rm = TRUE))
}
```

```{r run_synthetic_smap}
t0 <- Sys.time()
left_sm  <- nla_left_smap(y_syn,  L = 350, R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
right_sm <- nla_right_smap(y_syn, L = 150, R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
time_sm <- as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs")
combined_sm <- median(c(left_sm$tau_hat, right_sm$tau_hat), na.rm = TRUE)

tibble(estimate = c("True change point", "Left check", "Right check", "Combined"),
       value = c(cp_true, left_sm$tau_hat, right_sm$tau_hat, combined_sm))
```

## Comparison

```{r tbl-synthetic-comparison}
#| tbl-cap: "NLA-GP vs. NLA-S-map on the synthetic benchmark: accuracy and runtime."
tibble(Method = c("NLA-GP", "NLA-S-map"),
       `Left check` = c(left_gp$tau_hat, left_sm$tau_hat),
       `Right check` = c(right_gp$tau_hat, right_sm$tau_hat),
       Combined = c(combined_gp, combined_sm),
       `Error (vs. true)` = round(abs(c(combined_gp, combined_sm) - cp_true)),
       `Runtime (s)` = round(c(time_gp, time_sm), 1)) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

**We conclude:**

- **Right check** (test set = early, library shrinks from the late end): both methods find a clear valley, close to the true change point
- **Left check** (test set = late, library shrinks from the early end): NLA-S-map finds a valley here too; NLA-GP does not, because `K` drifts continuously -- more recent library data is always a bit more relevant regardless of the bifurcation, which masks the sharp before/after contrast the left check looks for
- On this benchmark, **NLA-S-map beats NLA-GP on both counts**: its combined estimate is closer to the true change point (error 12 vs. 28), and it runs faster (25.8s vs. 42.2s, @tbl-synthetic-comparison) -- the two-stage GP fitting trick pays off when hyperparameter search is the bottleneck, but for a low-dimensional system like this one, S-map's much simpler theta-search is already fast *and* it succeeded on both checks instead of one
- Takeaway: NLA-GP's real advantage is expected to show up on **more complex, higher-dimensional, or noisier** systems where GP-EDM's flexibility should out-predict a fixed-form local-linear model -- not necessarily on simple textbook cases like this one

# Empirical test

::: {.callout-tip title="Question"}
Lake Zurich shifted from a eutrophic to an oligotrophic state in the late 1980s. [Medeiros et al. 2025](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2416637122) dated this shift separately for all 13 plankton functional groups (@fig-medeiros-s17, @tbl-medeiros-s1). Does NLA-GP find similar timing, on the full monthly time series from Lake Zurich ([Merz et al. 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-023-01615-6))?
:::

## Data

**To answer this, we:**

- Process the raw monthly counts: interpolate a handful of missing months, z-score (`scale()`) each variable
- Use the **full** 1977-2020 series (no date restriction)
- Run NLA-GP (left + right check) on **all 13** functional groups

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**This section loads and processes the Lake Zurich data:**

- Builds a monthly date index, interpolates a few missing months
- Renames columns, z-scores each variable (`scale()`, no log-transform)
- `zurich_month_index()`: year/month -> row index, for marking reference dates
:::

```{r zurich_functions}
zurich_long_names <- c(
  Cy = "Cyanobacteria", Gr1 = "Green algae (small)", Gr2 = "Green algae (large)",
  Di1 = "Diatoms (small)", Di2 = "Diatoms (large)", Go1 = "Gold algae (small)",
  Go2 = "Gold algae (large)", Cr1 = "Cryptophytes (small)", Cr2 = "Cryptophytes (large)",
  Mi = "Mixotrophic flagellates", He = "Large herbivores", Om = "Omnivores",
  Pr = "Invertebrate predators", temperature = "Temperature", phosphorus = "Phosphate"
)

#' Load and process the raw Lake Zurich CSV (all available months): builds a
#' monthly time index, linearly interpolates the handful of scattered
#' single-month gaps, and z-scores each variable.
process_zurich_data <- function(path) {
  z <- read.csv(path)
  z <- z[order(z$year, z$month), ]
  z$time_idx <- seq_len(nrow(z))
  z$date <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", z$year, z$month))

  plankton_vars <- setdiff(names(zurich_long_names), c("temperature", "phosphorus"))
  for (v in c(plankton_vars, "temperature", "phosphorus")) {
    z[[v]] <- na.approx(z[[v]], x = z$time_idx, na.rm = FALSE)
  }
  z <- z[complete.cases(z[, plankton_vars]), ]

  for (v in plankton_vars) {
    z[[paste0("scaled_", v)]] <- as.numeric(scale(z[[v]]))
  }
  z$time_idx <- seq_len(nrow(z))
  rownames(z) <- NULL
  z
}

#' Row index closest to a given year-month, for marking reference dates.
zurich_month_index <- function(z, year, month) {
  target <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", year, month))
  which.min(abs(z$date - target))
}

z <- process_zurich_data(here("data", "raw", "lake_zurich.csv"))
```

![This figure was made by Medeiros et al. 2025 (their Fig. S17). Monthly time series for all 13 plankton functional groups (in ind/l), phosphate concentration (in mg/l), and water temperature (in Celsius) from Lake Zurich between January 1978 and December 2019. As explained in the Materials and Methods section in the main text, Medeiros et al. 2025 performed a change-point analysis to determine the location of a potential tipping point for each functional group independently. This potential tipping point is shown for each functional group as a black dashed line and Table S1 gives additional information.](figures/Fig.S17_Medeiros_2025.png){#fig-medeiros-s17}

  "Cr2", "Cryptophytes (large)",      "1996-02",    0.940,       0.024,

  "Go2", "Gold algae (large)",        "1987-06",    0.961,       0.049,

## Results

```{r run_zurich_all}
E <- 3; tau <- 1; Dskipstep <- 16; bandwidth <- 32
L_left <- 200; L_right <- 60
T_z <- nrow(z)

zurich_results <- pmap(table_s1, function(code, Group, `TP month`, `SS ratio`, Phosphate) {
  y <- z[[paste0("scaled_", code)]]
  ym <- as.integer(strsplit(`TP month`, "-")[[1]])
  ref_idx <- zurich_month_index(z, ym[1], ym[2])
  left <- nla_left(y, L = L_left, R = T_z, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  right <- nla_right(y, L = L_right, R = T_z, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  combined <- median(c(left$tau_hat, right$tau_hat), na.rm = TRUE)
  tibble(Group = Group, `Medeiros date` = `TP month`, `SS ratio` = `SS ratio`,
         `NLA-GP left` = left$tau_hat, `NLA-GP right` = right$tau_hat,
         `NLA-GP combined` = combined,
         `NLA-GP date` = if (is.na(combined)) NA_character_ else format(z$date[round(combined)], "%Y-%m"))
})
```

```{r tbl-zurich-summary}
#| tbl-cap: "NLA-GP detected change points vs. Medeiros et al. 2025 (Table S1), all 13 Lake Zurich functional groups, using the full 1977-2020 series and z-scored (not log-transformed) abundance."
zurich_summary <- bind_rows(zurich_results) %>% arrange(`SS ratio`)
knitr::kable(zurich_summary)
```

**We conclude:**

- Absolute timing differs from Medeiros et al.'s dates for most groups -- we would *not* claim precise agreement on the calendar date
- Medeiros et al.'s 3 clearest cases (lowest SS ratio: Green algae (large), Cryptophytes (small), Omnivores) are exactly the 3 groups we highlighted earlier; @tbl-zurich-summary shows how NLA-GP does on the full set of 13
- Consistent with our earlier (3-group) finding, NLA-GP's relative ordering of these 3 clearest groups still tracks Medeiros et al.'s

# Conclusion

- Implemented NLA-GP: Huang et al. 2024's NLA algorithm with GP-EDM instead of S-map (two-stage fitting, per Munch & Rogers)
- On a synthetic system with a **known** regime shift: NLA-GP's right check recovers it closely; its left check fails when the underlying parameter drifts continuously. NLA-S-map matched or beat NLA-GP on both accuracy and runtime on this simple benchmark
- On **real** Lake Zurich data (full series, all 13 groups, z-scored abundance): see @tbl-zurich-summary for how NLA-GP compares to Medeiros et al. 2025's change-point analysis

## Next

- Sensitivity analysis over `E`, `tau`, `Dskipstep`, and the smoothing bandwidth (we used one reasonable default throughout, not a tuned choice)
- Test NLA-GP vs. NLA-S-map on a higher-dimensional or noisier synthetic system, where GP-EDM's flexibility should matter more
- Apply NLA-GP to other empirical regime-shift datasets (e.g. Pacific Decadal Oscillation, per Huang et al. 2024 Sec. 3.2)
